books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War

options.misconception: The Proclamation ended all racial discrimination.
options.text: The end of all racial discrimination in the United States

options.misconception: The Proclamation gave all Black men in the North voting rights at once.
options.text: The immediate granting of voting rights to all Black men in the North
The passage of the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery

options.misconception: The Proclamation followed the repeal of the Fugitive Slave Act.
options.text: The repeal of the Fugitive Slave Act before the Civil War began

rationales.A: Racial discrimination did not end with the Proclamation.
rationales.B: Voting rights for Black men came unevenly and later.
rationales.C: The Proclamation paved the way for the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery nationwide. Emancipation as a war measure became emancipation as constitutional law, binding the whole nation.
rationales.D: The Fugitive Slave Act was not repealed before the war began.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what followed the Proclamation. A wartime measure needed a permanent settlement.
2. Name the settlement. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery nationwide.
3. Test the overstatements. Discrimination persisted, voting rights came unevenly, and the Fugitive Slave Act was not repealed before the war.
4. Connect the steps. The Proclamation made emancipation a war aim; the amendment made it law.
Remember: a wartime measure often needs a constitutional change to last.
